title: CAPs: Continuous Assembly Patterns
lede: What a CAP is, where you reverse, the two-hand version, and how it differs from a LOOP.
what-1: A CAP is the path of one prop, built from two or more simple curves joined end to end. A curve can be used more than once. The prop traces each piece in turn and comes back to where it started, so the whole path repeats.
what-2: Damien coined the term and published the construction on {0}, posting as Zaltymbunk and French_Saltimbanque.
what-3: The CAP drawn here has two halves. In the first, the hand carries the prop through half a circle while the prop keeps pointing away from the center. That is an extension. In the second, the hand comes back while the prop turns against it, drawing the inner petals. That is antispin. The prop ends in the same place and direction it started, so the path closes.
reverse-1: Damien wrote each piece of a CAP as a short line of numbers. The last one is a fraction: how much of the curve the prop uses before the next piece starts. That fraction is where you reverse.
reverse-2: His first worked example in the 2009 thread uses a half. Half a circle of extension, {0}, joins half a circle of antispin, {1}. That is the Yuta CAP, the pattern most spinners mean by "a cap" today. It takes its name from Yuta, the spinner whose moves the thread was analysing. In the same post Damien drew the two curves again at three quarters.
reverse-3: At a quarter, the same two curves give a quarter circle of extension and one antispin petal back. Each setting joins the curves at a different point, so each one draws a different closed shape with its own count of petals.
trace-2: Reverse after a half: the Yuta CAP
hands-1: Gage DeMello catalogued the two-hand version. One hand caps: it goes two beats on round the diamond and one beat back, changing its spin on the way back. The other hand keeps circling.
hands-2: Eight hand paths, with three spins for each hand, make 72 CAPs. The figure plays the first of them.

hand-caption: Left hand caps, right hand circles
loops-1: A CAP starts from one prop. Its path is built from simple curves, and each hand's path is worked out on its own. A two-hand pattern comes from putting two of those paths together.
loops-2: A LOOP starts from both hands at once. Each letter of the Kinetic Alphabet records where both hands and props go on one beat, and a LOOP is a word made of those letters that comes back to its starting position. The first Kinetic Alphabet guide called these CAPs too, which is why the two names get mixed up. They are covered in the {0}.
loop-note: a LOOP: both hands, turning a quarter each time it repeats
